Share pricing estimates and Dedicated vs Private TCO spreadsheet
Schedule on-site hardware sizing call with infra team
Follow up with SOC 2 / ISO docs and KMS/HSM integration notes

summary: Intro discovery for an on-prem, air-gapped deployment. Customer is highly regulated, requires offline updates, strict KMS/HSM control, and vendor-approved hardware. Discussed hardware constraints, update processes (USB/secure courier), no outbound connections, audit logs, SOC2/ISO, and a pilot benchmarking plan.
transcript: Meeting header: 2026-05-20 14:00 PST / Duration 48m / Attendees: Sam Carter (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Mark Li (CTO - Quanta Genomics), Elena Ruiz (Head of IT & Security), Javier Mendez (Infra)
[00:00] Sam Carter: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Sam, AE at Redwood, and with me is Priya, our solutions engineer. How are you all?
[00:06] Mark Li: Good thanks, Sam. We've been looking forward to this. We have a pretty strict set of requirements so wanted to walk through on-prem air-gapped options with you.

[00:14] Priya Desai: Great—happy to. Quick agenda: confirm requirements, current infra, update process for models/software, security questions (KMS, HSM, SSO), and then proposed POC steps. Sound good?

[00:23] Elena Ruiz: Yeah that's perfect. To start: we are regulated — clinical research / diagnostics — so no outbound network connectivity from our inference cluster. All updates must be done offline and approved. We also require HSM-backed keys and audit logs to satisfy audits.
[00:35] Sam Carter: Understood. When you say offline updates, can you describe current process? USBs, secure courier?

[00:40] Elena Ruiz: We generally use a controlled media transfer — encrypted HDDs couriered from our private build environment. We have strict chain-of-custody. So we need Redwood software and model artifacts to be installable via that flow. No automatic pull from internet during normal ops.

[00:52] Priya Desai: Okay that's common. Our Private deployment supports an air-gapped install pattern — control plane can be deployed in a customer-only network. We provide an installer bundle and signed model artifacts. Updates can be delivered as signed tarballs; you validate signatures using your HSM or external signing process. There's also an offline licensing/license token exchange mechanism. Quick note: some folks refer to it as 'air-gap bundle' in our docs.

[01:16] Javier Mendez: How do you handle model weights that are large? We run models that are 70-120GB per checkpoint. Shipping those over by disk is doable but the installer has to manage placement and verification. Do you support multi-file chunking and resume?

[01:29] Priya Desai: Yes. The distribution format supports chunked artifacts and checksums. During the install we run integrity verification. For very large models we can also provide quantized variants to reduce footprint. Also we support delta updates to reduce transfer size when patching a model version.

[01:43] Mark Li: Delta updates sound interesting. Our regulatory group will push back on any unexplained model behavior, so we also need clear provenance and an ability to pin model versions and roll back.

[01:51] Sam Carter: Absolutely. Pinning and immutable model versions are core to the Private offering — you can pin a model hash and we keep audit logs of every inference node and model loaded. Those logs can be shipped to your SIEM or kept locally; in air-gapped mode they'll be local files that you ingest into your auditor process.
[02:07] Elena Ruiz: On crypto: we use a hardware HSM from Thales/Entrust. Do you integrate with on-prem HSMs, or is Beacon (your key manager) mandatory?

[02:15] Priya Desai: We support both. Customers can use their on-prem HSMs via PKCS#11 for key unwrapping, or integrate with cloud KMS during non-air-gapped proof-of-concept phases. In your case, we would configure the node's key agent to call your HSM over the local network. No keys are exfiltrated.
[02:29] Javier Mendez: Does that require the control plane to reach out to Redwood-hosted services at any point?

[02:33] Priya Desai: No — for air-gapped installs the control plane is customer-managed. We do offer a private control plane variant where we ship the management components and you run them in your network. The only optional connectivity would be for Redwood support to fetch logs when you allow it via a temporary secure tunnel — but that's explicitly opt-in and auditable.
[02:49] Mark Li: Understood. What about model licensing and third-party model redistribution? We use some community models and some vendor-licensed weights. Do you have any guidance?

[02:56] Sam Carter: We'll need to confirm licensing with each model. For vendor-licensed weights we can support installing customer-provided artifacts only — that is, you supply the weight tarball and we help with the install. For open models in our catalog we can package them as part of the bundle if licensing permits. We'll document that in the security whitepaper we send.
[03:12] Elena Ruiz: SLA and maintenance windows: because this is offline we need planned maintenance procedures. How do you handle critical patching?

[03:19] Priya Desai: We provide patch bundles on the same air-gap path. For CVEs in the runtime we can provide hotfix images; your infra team reviews and applies them. For extremely urgent issues we recommend a short maintenance window with an agreed process for verifying the patch in a staging cluster first.

[03:33] Javier Mendez: Hardware — we're trying to standardize on NVIDIA A100 80GB but also evaluating H100. What are your recommendations for throughput/latency for typical LLM inference at sequence lengths of 1024 and concurrent QPS targets?

[03:45] Priya Desai: A100 80GB is a solid baseline. For batch-oriented workloads and high throughput, H100 gives a notable uplift especially for FP16/AMP. For 1024 tokens and a 1-2 token/sec per request expectation, one A100 can handle X — (note: numbers approximate) about 8-12 concurrent small requests with batching; H100 can be 1.5-2x depending on kernels and quantization. We'll produce a sizing doc with more precise numbers based on your prompt distribution.
[04:07] Mark Li: We run some heavy Gen and some short-form embeddings. Can we mix tasks on the same pool? We worry about QoS — embeddings can dominate throughput and affect latency for gen requests.

[04:16] Priya Desai: You can partition GPU pools by workload type, or implement qos routing rules. Redwood's runtime supports policy-based routing — you can pin routes to dedicated nodes or use priority queues for latency-sensitive workloads. For on-prem, you'd typically reserve a set of GPUs for low-latency gen and a different pool for batch embeddings.
[04:32] Elena Ruiz: Logging: need immutable audit logs, per-token cost visibility for internal chargebacks, and traceability for model input/outputs in case of issue. Any concerns re PHI?

[04:41] Sam Carter: We can configure audit logs to redact PII/PHI by default at ingestion, or keep raw logs within your cluster and apply your redaction pipeline. For compliance it's better you keep logs internal; Redwood's console can operate solely on metadata if desired. We'll include options in the doc.
[04:56] Mark Li: Ok timeline: we're aiming for a Q3 pilot with a small cluster and then a production rollout in Q4. What would you suggest for next steps?

[05:03] Sam Carter: Proposed next steps: 1) we'll send the air-gapped deployment guide + security whitepaper, 2) Priya will put together a preliminary hardware sizing and TCO for A100 vs H100, 3) schedule a hardware sizing deep-dive with Javier and Elena next week, and 4) start procurement/PO discussions after the sizing. Does that align?
[05:18] Elena Ruiz: Yes. Also please include a sample canary/rollback playbook — auditors will want to see a rollback plan specifically for model changes.

[05:25] Priya Desai: We'll add that. For the POC we typically do: baseline perf test with your representative prompts, a soak test for 48-72 hours, and security validation including signature verification workflow. For air-gapped POC we can ship a model bundle and a test harness that runs locally and uploads results back via an approved secure channel.
[05:44] Javier Mendez: One more thing: some of our sites are remote with low bandwidth. Are there strategies to reduce update size?

[05:50] Priya Desai: Delta updates, quantized models (8-bit / 4-bit where acceptable), and using smaller specialized models for low-bandwidth sites are common. Also dedupe model artifacts across multiple sites using a standard image so you only ship delta content.
[06:03] Mark Li: Compliance questions: do you have SOC 2 and ISO27001 artifacts we can share with our auditors? We also need penetration test results and a third-party risk assessment.

[06:12] Sam Carter: Yes — we have SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 paperwork; Priya will attach the docs. For penetration tests we can provide redacted reports and a summary of third-party risk assessments. In air-gapped mode, some items will be customer-controlled but we'll supply our secure development lifecycle artifacts.
[06:27] Elena Ruiz: What about support model? We need a dedicated TAM and the ability for emergency on-call escalation with a phone number; email SLA isn't enough for us.
[06:34] Sam Carter: For enterprise/private customers we offer TAM and a 24/7 escalation path as an add-on. We'll include support tiers and response SLAs in the proposal.

[06:42] Priya Desai: One more technical note — about model caching and K/V cache persistence. For inference with long conversations we rely on KV cache; in air-gapped clusters you can persist KV caches to shared storage to survive restarts, but you'll need to ensure the storage meets your encryption and retention policies.

[06:58] Javier Mendez: We're also curious about fallback strategies. If we can't reach support or need to rollback quickly, can we fallback to an on-prem smaller model that we ship and operate ourselves?

[07:06] Priya Desai: Yes — you can maintain a fallback model image in the cluster. Redwood's runtime supports multiple model slots and instant switch-over to a pinned image. We'll document recommended failover steps in the rollback playbook.
[07:18] Mark Li: Budget: we expect to fund Dedicated capacity plus the Private licensing. Please include capex estimates for hardware and a monthly/platform fee so we can present to procurement.
[07:25] Sam Carter: We'll assemble a draft TCO including hardware CAPEX (cards, servers, storage), Redwood Private license, and optional TAM/support fees.
[07:31] Elena Ruiz: Finally, data residency: model inputs may include patient data. We need assurance that nothing leaves the cluster, including temporary logs. Is that enforceable?

[07:40] Priya Desai: In air-gapped deployments all network egress is controlled by you; by default no telemetry leaves the cluster. We can also provide configurations to scrub or never persist certain fields. That will be in the security configuration guide we share.

[07:52] Sam Carter: Okay, to recap the next steps verbally: Sam sends proposal + TCO, Priya sends sizing and whitepaper, schedule hardware deep-dive with Javier/Elena, Elena to send infra inventory. We'll follow up and schedule the POC kickoff. Anything else?
[08:05] Mark Li: Please include the canary/rollback playbook and the exact process for offline signature verification.
[08:10] Sam Carter: Will do. Thanks everyone — we'll get these docs over by Friday.
[08:14] Elena Ruiz: Thanks, bye.
[08:15] End of meeting
